intake: agnostic - I take the question seriously and haven't settled it; I don't think the evidence gets you to a God, but I also don't think its absence gets you to no God, and I distrust how much I want a tidy answer either way

walk.note: As a description of how everyone actually starts, yes; that is how I started.
Testimony is evidence, just weak evidence, so the premise is overstated, but the conclusion that you look for God in the world rather than in the book is one I would take anyway.

The hiddenness dilemma mischaracterises Aquinas (his God has will), but the better half of the move, that the data bottoms out in testimony, texts and a bare first cause, carries me to doubt, which is where I live.
A failed prayer study refutes one interventionist model of God; a failed case gets an acquittal, not a finding of innocence, and atheism here is stated as a positive finding.
That mind does not seem to reduce to matter is a report of a seeming, and I would not sign up to two kinds of thing on a seeming.
Brain dependence and Elisabeth's question are the strongest material in the whole map.
'The only inside we know directly is experience' is a beautiful sentence, which is exactly why I distrust it; structure-not-intrinsic-nature gets you to a question, not to idealism.
Granting Dream, something is doing the dreaming; even Lichtenberg's 'it thinks' has thinking happening.
Strawson's point is right, though the move oddly reintroduces the brain after Dream set it aside.
This is my job description: treat well people whose insides you cannot verify and who may be lying to you; I would choose it.
Care given ahead of proof does keep the not-knowing in view; the correction clause about paternalism is the honest part.

The move concedes a secular hope and equanimity are equally open; I would take hope and leave the word faith on the table, and the author's own reason for hoping is a consequentialist one that does not need a maker.
The move's own last sentence says being a maker does not make a maker resolved, so the conclusion is withdrawn in the act of stating it.
'More of a bargain than an argument' is the whole move; I cannot tell what bargain or with whom.
The move itself admits the premise it needs, that to think is to ignore for any possible mind, has not been established against Aquinas.
Suffering is bad for the one who suffers whether or not anything stands behind it; I believed this before I read the map.
I take it as the question it honestly admits to being; the name Dualism is misleading for a position that is really 'continuity, unresolved'.
This is a stop, not a move; nothing is claimed that I could take or refuse, so I stop where the route stops.

first_exit.why: Absence of the evidence a particular interventionist God would leave is a case against that God, not against every God, and the hiddenness dilemma only bites if a God who is a subject is already ruled out, which nothing earlier did. In my work a failed case gets an acquittal, not a proof of innocence; the move treats doubt as if it were disbelief.

comment: Your standard of proof moves around: at move 4 absence of evidence is allowed to convict, while at move 16 you carefully refuse to let the same kind of absence convict Aquinas, and I think the second instinct is the right one for both. The places where the writing is most beautiful (move 8, move 13) are the places where the argument is thinnest, and I say that as someone who was moved by them and is suspicious of having been. Mercy at move 11 is the one step I would sign without hesitation, and it is also the one that honestly admits it needs no argument.
